desc:
This command lets you print a manual from the terminal and turn it into a PDF format. Read below on how it works:

Locates the raw text: The inner part $(man -w [command]) acts like a GPS. It finds the hidden folder where the system stores the manual's raw text.

Feeds the factory: The parent command mandoc grabs that raw text path immediately.

Formats the layout: The tool -T pdf works like a printing press. It takes the messy raw code and instantly formats it with clean headers, margins, and page breaks.

Delivers the physical file: The arrow > is a delivery chute. It shoots the finished, formatted document straight onto your Desktop as a real, permanent file.

Note: You can freely choose the destination file path of where you want the file to end up, doesn't always have to be your Desktop folder.

This script (with the right commands) allows you to export a command manual from the terminal and print it as a .txt file. This helps with reading the manual entirely without relying on the Mac terminal to review the entire manual.

Example:

user@macbook-air ~ % man zsh | col -b > zsh-manual.txt

This will create a text file of the zsh's shell language for its manual so you can freely ready it at your own pace.

This command allows you to open a file using the default program the file type is set to open with by default.

Example:

user@macbook-air ~ % open dummy.txt

Result: The file will open with the TextEditor app if your .txt file is set to open with said app by default.

Do you want to know where you currently are in the terminal?

Use pwd

Example:

pwd outputs /Users/yourusername 

This says you currently are in your own user folder.

The mv command (short for "move") relocates files or folders from one place to another, or renames them in place.

Key Uses:

* Rename Files or Folders: Changes the name of a file or directory without changing its content or location.
* Move Files or Folders: Shifts items into a different directory on your system.
* Overwrite Files: Moves a file into a location where a file with the same name already exists (replacing it).

Example:

Rename a file

mv index.html home.html

Move a file into a subfolder

mv home.html src/

Rename and move a file at the same time

mv home.html src/index.html

The cat command (short for "concatenate") reads one or more files and displays their full content directly in the terminal, or merges multiple files into a single file.

Key Uses:

View File Content: Quickly displays what is inside a file without opening an editor.

Combine Files: Merges the contents of multiple files into a new file.

Create File with Multiple Lines: Writes multi-line content into a new file from the terminal.

Example:

View the contents of a file
cat index.html

Combine two files into a third file
cat header.html body.html > fullpage.html

The echo command prints text to your terminal screen, or redirects that text to create or add content to files.

Key Uses:

Print Text: Displays a message or variable value directly in the terminal window.

Create or Overwrite File (>): Writes text into a file, replacing any existing content.

Append to File (>>): Adds text to the end of an existing file without deleting current content.

Example:

Create a file with initial content
echo "Hello World" > index.html

Add a new line to the bottom of an existing file
echo "New paragraph" >> index.html

The touch command creates new, empty files quickly or updates the modification timestamp on existing files without changing their content.

Key Uses:

Create Empty Files: Generates a blank file of any extension (like .html, .txt, .js) if the file does not exist yet.

Update Timestamps: Sets an existing file's "last modified" time to the current date and time.

Example:

touch index.html

You can also create multiple files at once:

touch style.css app.js index.html

This command allows you to zip files of any kind. To use it, use this example:

To zip a text file use: zip dummy.zip dummy.txt 

Please note that each file name is a just a reference on the order the file names must go in the terminal.
This command lists the current directory content in its current location, unless a path is specified in the command.

The nano command opens a lightweight, beginner-friendly text editor directly inside your terminal window. It allows you to quickly create, view, or modify code and configuration files without launching a separate graphical application.

The rm -f command forcefully and permanently deletes files without asking for confirmation or sending them to the Trash. The **`-f`** (force) flag bypasses read-only warnings and silences error messages if the targeted file does not exist.
